source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Core thesis. Amnesic treatments after training or after reactivation do not erase the memory. They create new learning that interferes with the original. The original then depends on retrieval cues to be expressed.
numbers: Preprint doi 10.31234/osf.io/zjxvu. Published Psych Rev 133(2):411-449 (2026), doi 10.1037/rev0000538. A review: no new data.
quote: memory retrieval is a critical component of memory performance
limits: Written by advocates (Miller, Urcelay). 'Most if not all' is a strong claim. Non-recovery cases are explained by narrow parameters.
agent_relevance: A failed answer is not proof the knowledge is gone. The agent should try several cues before it calls something unknown.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Table 1 map. Deficits from extinction, counterconditioning, retrieval-induced forgetting, cue interference, cue competition, post-training amnesia and cue-induced amnesia are said to recover with the same few manipulations: time passage, physical context, state context, CS or retrieval cue, US reminder.
numbers: Table 1 lists cell citations. Several cells are empty (never tested), e.g. no US-reinstatement recovery found for proactive or retroactive outcome interference.
limits: A literature map, not a meta-analysis. No pooled effect sizes. Publication bias not assessed.
agent_relevance: A checklist of cue types to try when retrieval fails: delay, original context, internal state, partial cue, strong reminder.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Sissons and Miller (2009): A+ then B+/BA- versus the reverse order. Tested right after phase 2, behavior follows the most recent training. After a 27-day interval the first-learned association dominates. So second-learned information is what depends on context and time.
numbers: 27-day retention interval; rats. Group sizes not given in the review.
limits: Second-hand summary of a rat study.
agent_relevance: Newest information is easiest to reach. Old information returns when the cue context shifts. Keep old and new facts as separate dated items rather than overwriting.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Escobar, Matute and Miller (2001) retroactive cue interference: X+ in one context, Y+ in another. Testing X in Y's context gave strong interference. Testing X in X's own context gave little. This is the same logic as ABA renewal after extinction. Proactive interference also recovers with time and with reminders (Amundson 2003; Urcelay and Miller 2010).
numbers: Rat conditioning; numbers not given in the review.
limits: Review summary only.
agent_relevance: Interference between similar items is cue-gated. Context tags at write time and at query time decide which item wins.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Cue competition (overshadowing, blocking, overexpectation) also recovers. Time attenuates overshadowing (Miller, Jagielo and Spear 1990) and blocking (Batsell 1997). Retrieval cues recover overshadowing (Cole 1999). A CS presentation recovers blocking (Schachtman 1983).
numbers: Animal studies; numbers are in the original papers, not in the review.
limits: Some Table 1 cells are inferred by the authors.
agent_relevance: Items that lose to a salient competitor at encoding are not necessarily missing. A targeted cue can bring them back.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Retrieval-induced forgetting (Anderson, Bjork and Bjork 1994) has an inhibition account and two interference accounts. All three say retrieval at test is altered. RIF vanished after a 24 h delay in some studies and with a context change (Jonker 2013), but not in others (Maxcey 2021; Soares 2016). Relearning was faster for suppressed items (Storm, Bjork and Bjork 2008).
numbers: Murayama et al. (2014) meta-analysis is cited for retention-interval effects; its value is not quoted in the review.
limits: Mixed evidence on whether RIF depends on context. The authors lean on the positive cases.
agent_relevance: Repeated retrieval on one branch can make its siblings harder to reach. Do not conclude a sibling is absent after heavy retrieval of its neighbor.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Nairne (2002) qualifier: what matters is the diagnostic value of a cue, meaning how well it picks the target out from competitors, not raw encoding-retrieval overlap. Example: a school uniform cue helps in a room of adults and not in a cafeteria of schoolboys.
numbers: Conceptual. Example credited to Goh and Tan (2006).
limits: Cue-overload is a competing and complementary account to encoding specificity.
agent_relevance: Cue design rule: score a cue by how many competing items it also matches, not only by how well it matches the target.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: The storage view of amnesia. Muller and Pilzecker (1900): recall of syllable pairs suffered when a new list followed within about a minute. Duncan (1949): ECS up to 15 min after rat avoidance learning caused amnesia, but not beyond 1 h. Inhibitors of protein synthesis (puromycin, anisomycin, cycloheximide) later gave the same time-graded pattern.
numbers: ECS-to-learning interval: amnesia at 15 min or less, none beyond 1 h (Duncan 1949).
limits: The temporal gradient is the main evidence for consolidation. The review argues recovery data break the permanent-loss reading.
agent_relevance: Names the claim under attack: 'gone' versus 'not reachable'.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Reconsolidation claim. Nader, Schafe and LeDoux (2000): anisomycin in the amygdala after reactivation caused amnesia for fear memory, not without reactivation, not when delayed 6 h. Duvarci and Nader (2004) found no spontaneous recovery (test 23 days later), no ABC renewal and no reinstatement after anisomycin. The review notes they tested the memory before the recovery manipulation, and Wheeler and Miller (2007) show such a prior test can block recovery.
numbers: Rats, tone-shock; test at 23 days; 6 h delay = no amnesia.
limits: The review argues non-recovery may come from narrow parameters and the intermediate test, so it is weak evidence for erasure.
agent_relevance: An early probe of an uncertain answer can change what later cues recover. Keep first-pass probes cheap and separate from the final recall attempt.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Recovery from post-training amnesia has been reported since the 1960s: spontaneous recovery over time (Cooper and Koppenaal 1964; Zinkin and Miller 1967; Quartermain 1970, 1972), US reinstatement (Misanin, Miller and Lewis 1968), CS reminder (Deweer and Sara 1981), and re-giving the amnesic as a state cue (Overton 1964; Hinderliter 1975; Bradley and Galal 1988).
numbers: Per-study numbers are not in the review.
limits: Mostly 1960s-80s rodent work with small groups and varied parameters.
agent_relevance: The oldest cue-design idea: re-create the state in which the memory was laid down.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Miller and Springer ECS work: ECS given 0.3 s after a single training session left performance intact 15 min later, but poor at longer delays. Lewis, Miller and Misanin (1969): prior familiarization with the apparatus reduced the ECS deficit even when ECS followed a 0.5 s shock. So a usable memory formed within about 0.5 s, before any consolidation window could act.
numbers: 0.3 s ECS delay, 15 min test; 0.5 s shock; 10 s footshock in Miller and Springer; rats.
limits: The interpretation is the authors'. Consolidation theorists treat short-lived traces as a different store.
agent_relevance: Memory forms at once; what varies is later access. This maps to an agent that writes instantly but must index well.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Human cue-induced amnesia is weak. Walker et al. (2003) motor sequence reminder gave about a 50% accuracy drop on day 3, but Hardwicke et al. (2016) failed to replicate. Hupbach 2007 and 2009: the reminded group did not lose list 1 but intruded list 2 items. Schiller 2010 reported fear stayed low for a year; later tests largely failed (Chan 2010; Chalkia 2020; Jaswetz 2022; Luyten and Beckers 2017). Propranolol effects held for startle but not for skin conductance or expectancy ratings.
numbers: Walker: about -50% accuracy. Kroes 2014: ECS patients scored worse on the reactivated story than the other story. Kroes 2010: 40 mg propranolol, 90 min before test.
limits: The authors admit boundary conditions have piled up (trace strength, memory age, prediction error) and replication is poor.
agent_relevance: Human 'rewrite by reminder' effects are unreliable. Do not build the scaffold on reconsolidation-style tricks.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Prediction error is the proposed gate for destabilization. Rescorla-Wagner: learning scales with the gap between outcome and summed expectation. Mackintosh uses stimulus-specific error. Pearce-Hall uses unsigned error to set attention. Rescorla-Wagner has one associative strength and cannot predict recovery from extinction.
numbers: Formal models: Rescorla and Wagner 1972; Mackintosh 1975; Pearce and Hall 1980. Modirshanechi, Brea and Gerstner (2022) list many error formalisations.
limits: Review summary. The link from prediction error to destabilization is itself contested.
agent_relevance: A mismatch between expected and found content is the trigger to open a record for rewriting. Possible link to the schema's check-failure signal (G1).

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Memory integration account (Gisquet-Verrier and Riccio): the internal state caused by the amnesic drug at reactivation is bound into the memory. At test the state is missing, so retrieval fails. Prediction: give the same drug again before test and amnesia reverses. Supported for cycloheximide, LiCl, hypothermia (recooling before test, Mactutus 1982).
numbers: Cycloheximide systemic and local, LiCl, hypothermia; rodents.
limits: A close rival of the 'new learning' account. They are not identical.
agent_relevance: State-dependent retrieval: re-create the exact framing and format used at write time.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Engram rescue findings. Ryan et al. 2015: light on engram cells reversed anisomycin amnesia. Similar rescues in early-Alzheimer mice (Roy 2016), infantile amnesia (Guskjolen 2018), sleep deprivation (Bolsius 2023), subconcussive impact (Chapman 2024), retroactive interference (Autore 2023). Nabavi 2014: optogenetic LTD in amygdala inputs caused amnesia and LTP restored fear.
numbers: Seven rodent models listed; counts are in the primary papers.
limits: All rodent. Optogenetic activation is an artificial cue. The authors say the biological basis of the engram is still uncertain.
agent_relevance: Direct proof that 'cannot recall with the natural cue' and 'cannot recall with any cue' differ. Motivates a cue-search stage before an answer is called unknown.

source: Ryan, Roy, Pignatelli, Arons and Tonegawa (2015) Engram cells retain memory under retrograde amnesia. Science
finding: Mice with a labeled dentate gyrus engram were trained in contextual fear. Anisomycin after training caused amnesia with natural cues. Light on the labeled engram cells produced freezing equal in anisomycin and saline groups. Spine density and synaptic strength of engram cells were lower under anisomycin.
numbers: Natural recall ANI < SAL, p<0.005 (Test 1), p<0.05 (Test 2). Light-on freezing significant in SAL p<0.01 and ANI p<0.05, no group difference. DG n=10 ANI vs 12 SAL; CA1 n=9/10; amygdala tone n=9/9; reconsolidation design n=11/11 (ANI < SAL, p<0.01 at Test 2). Amygdala c-Fos n=3-4 per group. Chance overlap 0.76 (CA3) and 0.42 (BLA).
limits: Exact freezing percentages appear only in figures. Small n (3-12). Artificial stimulation is not natural recall.
agent_relevance: Storage can survive while natural-cue access fails. Supports separating write from access in an agent memory and testing alternative access routes.

source: Roy et al. (2016) Memory retrieval by activating engram cells in mouse models of early Alzheimer's disease. Nature
finding: Early-AD mouse models (APP/PS1 and 3xTg) were amnesic with natural cues. Light activation of engram cells retrieved the memory. Amnesia tracked lower spine density in DG engram cells. Optogenetic LTP at perforant path synapses restored spines and memory, and anisomycin blocked the rescue.
numbers: APP/PS1 at 7 months (no plaques) and 9 months (plaques). Spines counted: 7,032 (AD) vs 9,437 (control), n=4 mice per group. Memory rescue n=10, F(1,36)=4.95 P<0.05. Inhibitory avoidance F(1,27)=25.22 P<0.001. Novel object F(1,56)=5.87 P<0.05. In vitro LTP in 6 of 30 cells, EPSP +10%.
limits: Mouse models only. Group freezing values are in figures, not text. Human early-AD amnesia may differ.
agent_relevance: Retrieval-not-storage applied to disease. Analogy: weak recall may be an index problem, not a missing fact.

source: Gisquet-Verrier et al. (2015) Integration of new information with active memory accounts for retrograde amnesia. J Neurosci 35:11623
finding: Cycloheximide after inhibitory-avoidance training or reactivation caused amnesia. A reminder, or re-giving the same drug before test, reversed it. LiCl, which does not block protein synthesis, gave the same pattern. Memory can form and be used with protein synthesis largely blocked.
numbers: Cyclo 2.8 mg/kg. Exp1a: group F(3,30)=8.05; amnesia F(1,15)=28.39 p<.001; reminder reversed F(1,15)=8.40 p<.01. Exp2a (reactivation): amnesia F(1,17)=8.78 p<.01; re-injection group vs control F<1; reversal F(1,18)=7.945 p<.01. ICV Exp3 n=34, reinfusion F(1,11)=5.86 p<.05. LiCl 300 mg/kg: amnesia F(1,18)=72.39; re-injection F(1,16)=7.43 p=.014. Protein synthesis inhibition 72% at 30 min, 68% at 1 h; LiCl +3% and +5%. Groups of 5-11.
limits: Two labs, small groups, the lab that proposed the integration view. Some recovery partial (Exp1b p=.03). Text has stats typos (Exp1a F=6.20 with p=0.23).
agent_relevance: Concrete test of state-dependent retrieval: restoring the original internal state removes the deficit. For an agent: match prompt and format between write and read.

source: Alfei, De Gruy, De bundel, Luyten and Beckers (2020) Generalization and recovery of post-retrieval amnesia. J Exp Psychol Gen
finding: Midazolam after context re-exposure causes amnesia for contextual fear in rats. The amnesia generalizes to a similar context B, but recovers when tested in the original context A or a new context C. This challenges both erasure and a simple memory-integration account.
numbers: Exp1 N=32 (8/group): ABA froze more, F(3,28)=8.11 p<.001 eta2p=.46. Exp2 N=24, MDZ 3 mg/kg: Kruskal-Wallis H(2)=12.68 p=.002; retest F(2,21)=15.39 p<.001. Exp3 N=48: interaction F(2,42)=3.66 p=.03; AAB d=1.90; ABB d=1.72; ABA d=0.08 (no amnesia in A). Exp4 N=16 d=1.96. Exp5 N=56: only AAA-Shift/MDZ differed, p=.002.
limits: Rats, 8 per group, one drug. Raw freezing means only in figures. Author list in source field taken from the review citation (Alfei et al. 2020), middle names unverified.
agent_relevance: Amnesia specific to one test context and absent in another means the item is still there. Test a fact under varied framings before judging it lost.

source: Hardwicke, Taqi and Shanks (2016) Postretrieval new learning does not reliably induce human memory updating via reconsolidation. PNAS
finding: Four direct replications of Walker et al. (2003) found no reminder-induced impairment. Three conceptual replications with declarative recall also found none. Retrieval seemed to help preserve the memory.
numbers: Original (group 7, n=16): accuracy about -57% (read off a figure). Replications n=16 each, N=64: accuracy change +3.13, +0.08, -1.98, -2.64 percent; BF01 8.97, 5.38, 1.90, 1.85. Pooled BF01 5.74 (accuracy), 36.0 (speed). Conceptual Exps 5-7 N=48: reminder vs no-reminder t(26.59)=-1.409, P=.915 one-tailed.
limits: Motor sequence and recall tasks only. Replicators are skeptics.
agent_relevance: Strong human evidence against the classic reminder-then-new-learning weakening. The retrieval-failure case must rest on cue manipulations, not reminders alone.

source: Kredlow, Unger and Otto (2016) Harnessing reconsolidation to weaken fear and appetitive memories: a meta-analysis of post-retrieval extinction effects. Psychological Bulletin
finding: Pooled 63 comparisons of post-retrieval extinction versus standard extinction. Small-to-moderate benefit for humans, large for appetitive responses in animals, small and nonsignificant for fear in animals.
numbers: 63 comparisons. Humans fear g=0.40. Animal appetitive g=0.89. Animal fear g=0.21 (nonsignificant). Moderators: number of animals housed together; time between extinction and test. Search ran to June 2014.
limits: Abstract only (full text blocked by a browser check). Search ended in 2014, before the main failed replications.
agent_relevance: Pooled evidence for reminder-based updating is modest, and weakest in animal fear where it began.

source: Appraising reconsolidation theory and its empirical validation (2023) Psychonomic Bulletin and Review; authors not verified
finding: Critique of reconsolidation theory. Contradictory findings and replication failures exist. The theory and its boundary conditions are vaguely defined, which makes it close to impossible to refute. Calls for caution before assuming a reconsolidation process underlies findings.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers.
limits: Abstract-level read via Europe PMC record.
agent_relevance: Warning against a mechanism that explains everything and so predicts nothing. Test cue effects directly.

source: Verification report of Schiller et al. (2010), Cortex 2020: Preventing the return of fear in humans using reconsolidation update mechanisms; authors not verified
finding: Re-analysis of Schiller et al. (2010) with the original data. Every reported group difference in fear recovery depended on qualitative participant exclusions. With principled exclusions, fear recovery was similar after reactivation-extinction and standard extinction. Experiment 2 differences did not verify.
numbers: Seven analysis sets (3 replicating the original, 4 with principled exclusions). Numbers per set not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only; the full text was blocked.
agent_relevance: A famous effect can rest on analyst choices. Fix inclusion rules before looking at scaffold comparison results.

source: Nader, Schafe and LeDoux (2000) Fear memories require protein synthesis in the amygdala for reconsolidation after retrieval. Nature 406:722
finding: Anisomycin in the lateral and basal amygdala after reactivation caused later amnesia for auditory fear, whether reactivation was 1 or 14 days after conditioning. No reactivation left memory intact. A 6 h delay gave no amnesia.
numbers: Reactivation at 1 or 14 days; infusion delayed 6 h = no amnesia.
limits: Abstract only. Group sizes not read. Later work shows such amnesia can recover under cues.
agent_relevance: This is the erasure-on-retrieval claim the retrieval-failure view rebuts. Know which claim not to rely on.

source: Warrington and Weiskrantz (1970) Amnesic syndrome: consolidation or retrieval? Nature 228:628
finding: Amnesic patients retained verbal material when tested with partial-information cues. Retention depended more on the retrieval method than on the acquisition method. Long-term memory showed up when the test removed incorrect and interfering responses.
numbers: Paywalled: abstract and reference list read only. Page lists 784 citations. Cites Warrington and Weiskrantz 1968 (Nature 217:972) and Tulving and Pearlstone 1966.
quote: Amnesic patients can remember verbal material if they are tested with a method of partial information.
limits: Abstract only, no numbers. Later work split this into spared implicit memory versus impaired explicit memory.
agent_relevance: Founding human result for cue design: fragment cues reveal memory that free recall misses, and cues that cut competitors matter.

source: Tulving and Pearlstone (1966) Availability versus accessibility of information in memory for words. J Verbal Learning Verbal Behavior 5:381
finding: As described by Alfei et al.: participants learned categorized word lists, then free recall, then cued recall. Words missed in free recall were recovered with category cues. So many failures are of accessibility, not availability.
numbers: Primary not opened (publisher returned 403). No numbers recorded.
limits: Secondary description only. Do not cite figures from this line.
agent_relevance: Free-recall misses are not proof of absence. Offer category names as cues before concluding a fact is missing.

source: Tulving and Thomson (1973) Encoding specificity and retrieval processes in episodic memory. Psychological Review 80:352
finding: As described by Alfei et al.: the encoding specificity principle says retrieval depends on the match between encoding and retrieval conditions. Tulving, Le Voi, Routh and Loftus (1983) revived Semon's 'ecphory' for the interaction of trace and cue.
numbers: Primary not opened. Covered by the earlier deep document 01_encoding_specificity.
limits: Overlaps the earlier document; see it for numbers.
agent_relevance: Foundation for matching cue to write context. See subfields 01 and 02.

source: Miller and Springer (1973) Amnesia, consolidation, and retrieval. Psychological Review 80:69
finding: As quoted by Alfei et al. (p. 73): recovery studies indicate that at least some experimental amnesia is retrieval failure. This is the 1973 root of the view.
numbers: Primary not opened (no abstract in Europe PMC).
quote: collectively, these recovery of memory studies indicate that at least some instances of experimental amnesia are cases of retrieval failure
limits: Quote taken from the Alfei review.
agent_relevance: The early review that the 2025 paper revives. Anchor for citations.

source: Gisquet-Verrier and Riccio (2018) Memory integration as a challenge to the consolidation/reconsolidation hypothesis. Front Syst Neurosci 12:71
finding: Verbal model. During an active (new or reactivated) memory, salient information, including the drug-induced internal state, is integrated into the memory. Amnesia is the absence of that state at test. Predictions: delayed onset, reversal by reminders (best by re-inducing the state), less effect after strong training or pre-exposure. Differs from reconsolidation: no destabilization or restabilization, no protein-synthesis need, memory modified not erased.
numbers: Page text says memories form and are retrieved even when 'more than 80%' of protein synthesis is blocked (the lab's own claim, not verified here).
limits: Read 100,000 of 130,186 characters. No new data. Authors are the proponents.
agent_relevance: Gives a testable cue model: record state at write; reproduce it at read.

source: Stout and Miller (2007) SOCR (sometimes opponent process comparator) model, as cited by Alfei et al. 2025
finding: Alfei et al. cite Stout and Miller (2007) as a theory that uses prediction error at training and a retrieval-stage comparison to turn associative strength into performance. Miller and Matzel's comparator view makes performance depend on the target link relative to competing links.
numbers: Primary not opened.
limits: Secondary description. Details of the model not verified.
agent_relevance: Retrieval as a comparison against rivals fits the cue-overload idea. Score retrieval by margin over competitors.

source: Alfei, Miller, Ryan and Urcelay (2025) Rethinking memory impairments: Retrieval failure. Psychological Review (preprint full text, 133 pp)
finding: Adaptive forgetting. Miller (2021) argues impaired retrieval of tangential information beats erasure because what is tangential today may matter tomorrow. Autore et al. (2023): retroactive interference in mice made the original engram less likely to reactivate, an interference engram dominated, and optogenetic reactivation rescued the forgotten memory. Fear memories lose precision over time (Wiltgen 2010).
numbers: Mouse object-context task; no counts in the review.
quote: If we remembered everything, we should on most occasions be as ill off as if we remembered nothing.
limits: Review framing; evidence mostly rodent. Quote is William James (1890) as cited by the review.
agent_relevance: Do not try to retrieve everything. Gating is a feature. The fix is a better way to ask, not a bigger memory dump.
